newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Cartier jewels exceed estimates at Geneva sales.
newsitem.headline: Cartier jewels exceed estimates at Geneva sales.

text.p: Jewels and watches by the renowned French house Cartier were going for higher than their estimates on Tuesday, with bidders keen to secure a piece of history.

The auction of more than 600 pieces by Cartier, held jointly by Geneva's Antiquorum Auctioneers and the Parisian Etude Tajan, took off after a pair of diamond hoop earrings soared to 200,000 Swiss francs ($150,000) -- more than three times their estimate.
The one-day sale was billed as a world premiere, with Cartier offering certificates of authenticity to the new owners.

"Their pitch is credible. They are selling the history of the firm. It is one of the first opportunities to purchase this type of 20th Century artefact," Edward Faber, a dealer on New York's Fifth Avenue, told Reuters in the auction room.
The crowd of buyers from Asia, Europe, and the United States burst into applause as the stunning loops from the 1930's Art Deco period were sold in a luxury hotel along Lake Geneva.
"Prices are very strong. Bids are coming in by telephone from all over the world," Gloria Teresi of Antiquorum Auctioneers told Reuters.
Prototype Cartier watches from limited editions went for several times their pre-sale estimate, according to Teresi.
A 1996 pink gold digital gentleman's wristwatch, from a limited series of three by Cartier for this event and estimated to fetch between $12,000 and $15,000, soared to $75,000.
A 1996 platinum rectangular digital gentleman's wristwatch, which had been expected to also fetch between $19,000 and $23,000, was finally sold for more than $60,000.
"The new prototype watches did extremely well," Faber said.
Among the Cartier works on the block is a stunning Indian-style platinum necklace set with 29 emeralds worn by exotic British film star Merle Oberon. It is expected to fetch $1.5 million.
Cartier pieces which once belonged to Egypt's King Farouk, Morocco's King Hassan, the late pop artist Andy Warhol and Woolworth heiress Barbara Hutton are also up for grabs.
A yellow gold Chinese clock designed as a pagoda, made by Cartier in 1989 and set with 2,471 diamonds, 55 emeralds as well as other gems, is expected to go for $650,000-$750,000.

Later in the evening at Christie's, a Bulgari gold necklace worn by Sharon Stone in the film "Casino" and other dazzling designer jewels belonging to a jet-set Lebanese divorcee are seeking new owners (eds: starts 1800 GMT).

The sale of the personal collection of Mouna al-Ayoub, the glamorous Lebanese former wife of Saudi businessman Nasser Al-Rachid, is expected to bring in between $8 million-$10 million, according to Christie's.
The mother of five, who is parting with 146 lots, viewed the collection in Geneva at the weekend, but has since returned to see her children in Saudi Arabia, according to a Christies' spokeswoman.
"The sale looks very good because there has been strong interest in her jewels. We hope to sell 100 per cent of the lots," the spokeswoman told Reuters.
"She will be giving part of the proceeds to a certain number of foundations and medical institutes in Europe and the United States," she added.
Press reports say the 39-year-old intends to give part of the money raised to a charity foundation in Majorca.

A Bulgari three-row beaded necklace, matching bracelet and pair of earrings -- worn by the steamy Stone in Martin Scorsese's film "Casino" last year -- is estimated to go for between $10,000 and $15,000.
